title: POC scoping: Quantiva SIEM-ready audit export + EU data residency
summary: Quantiva is evaluating Redwood’s SIEM-ready audit export beta as a gating control for production rollout. Primary concerns: (1) EU data residency (audit logs + export path must remain in EU), (2) reliable delivery semantics with dedup/idempotency for their SIEM ingestion, (3) ability to filter categories/actions to reduce noise and avoid PII, and (4) operational visibility (export lag, last success/error) for SOC. Redwood confirmed beta supports Splunk HEC, Datadog Logs, and S3 delivery with at-least-once semantics and stable event_id. Quantiva prefers S3 in their EU account as first path, with potential Splunk later. Agreed success criteria and next steps: share schema v2 + field allowlist/redaction policy, confirm EU-region-only deployment details for hosted/dedicated, and schedule a short technical validation focused on S3 IAM/KMS and filter configuration.
topics: Quantiva SIEM requirements and current tooling (SOC workflows, ingestion patterns)
EU data residency constraints (where audit events are stored/processed, exporter region)
Delivery guarantees (at-least-once, checkpointing, retries, DLQ, dedup expectations)
Filtering model (categories/actions, allowlist vs denylist, safe defaults)
PII minimization (what is and isn’t included in audit events; IP/user agent questions)
S3 destination specifics (cross-account role, SSE-KMS, partitioning, backfill window)
Beta scope/limitations (hosted + dedicated only, feature-flag allowlist, backfill cap)
questions: Can Redwood guarantee audit export processing stays entirely in EU (control plane + exporter + storage), and can that be evidenced for procurement?
What is the backfill limit for the beta and how does replay work after a downstream outage?
Do audit events include prompt text or generated output (Quantiva preference: no), and how are IP/user agent handled?
How should Quantiva deduplicate events in Splunk/S3 pipelines (event_id, ordering guarantees)?
Can filters be managed by a limited admin role (RBAC) without giving full account admin access?
What metrics/dashboards will Quantiva be able to view (lag, delivery success, last error)?
action_items: Simran Kaur (Redwood): Send Quantiva the SIEM audit export beta security FAQ + retention vs export responsibilities language (by 2025-04-04).
Colin O'Donnell (Redwood): Share S3 integration notes (required IAM assume-role policy, SSE-KMS options, example bucket policy) and propose a 30-min technical validation session (by 2025-04-04).
Naomi Feldman (Redwood): Confirm beta eligibility timeline + tenant allowlist process and communicate expected beta start window (by 2025-04-05).
Elena Varga (Quantiva): Provide preferred AWS region(s) for the S3 bucket (e.g., eu-central-1 vs eu-west-1) and whether cross-account role is acceptable (by 2025-04-05).
Jonas Keller (Quantiva): Share expected audit event volume (rough requests/day, number of admin users) and their current SIEM parsing expectations (by 2025-04-08).
next_steps: Schedule S3 delivery technical deep dive (Quantiva Platform + Security + Redwood SE).
Redwood to share audit event schema v2 example payloads + category taxonomy and filtering examples.
Quantiva to confirm EU residency requirements in writing (which components must be EU-only: storage, processing, support access).
Align on POC success criteria and the exact validations needed for Quantiva’s internal security sign-off.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-04-02
Start time: 14:03 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Title: POC scoping: Quantiva SIEM-ready audit export + EU data residency

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Simran Kaur (Solutions Architect), Colin O'Donnell (Solutions Engineer), Naomi Feldman (PM)
Quantiva: Elena Varga (Security Engineering), Tomás Ribeiro (Platform Lead), Marie Dubois (DPO), Jonas Keller (SOC Lead)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer wants SIEM export for audit logs with EU-only data residency.
- Preferred destination is S3 first, potential Splunk later.
- Discussed at-least-once delivery and event_id for dedup.
- Agreed on success criteria and follow-ups.


[00:00] Simran Kaur: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Simran from Redwood. I’ve got Colin here, and Naomi who owns the beta program for the audit export.
[00:10] Simran Kaur: Goal today is basically: understand your SIEM needs, the residency constraints, and then scope what a POC would look like if we include you in the beta cohort.
[00:20] Elena Varga: Yep. Thanks Simran. We can keep it pretty direct. We’re blocked on rolling Redwood into production unless we can get audit events into our SIEM in a reliable way.
[00:31] Jonas Keller: And visibility. Like we need to know if it’s lagging, if it’s failing, who changed what. The usual.
[00:37] Tomás Ribeiro: Also, EU region only. That’s non negotiable for our regulated environments.

[00:46] Simran Kaur: Got it. Maybe quick intros on your side too?
[00:50] Elena Varga: Elena, security engineering. I manage integrations like audit pipelines.
[00:55] Jonas Keller: Jonas, SOC lead. We’re on Splunk today for most security logs but we also have Datadog for infra logs.
[01:02] Marie Dubois: Marie, DPO. I’m here mainly to understand what personal data is in the audit events and where it travels.
[01:09] Tomás Ribeiro: Tomás, platform. I’d be implementing whatever role/bucket/policy you need.

[01:15] Simran Kaur: Perfect. Naomi, do you want to give the quick “what is the beta” context?
[01:20] Naomi Feldman: Sure. So we’re in beta for what we call SIEM-ready audit export. It’s basically: canonical audit event schema, plus an exporter service that can deliver to Splunk HEC, Datadog logs intake, or S3.
[01:34] Naomi Feldman: It’s feature-flagged per tenant. We’re keeping the cohort small, like three to five accounts, so we can iterate on the rough edges.
[01:41] Naomi Feldman: For beta specifically: hosted and dedicated deployments are in scope; private/on-prem is not in scope for beta.

[01:49] Tomás Ribeiro: That’s fine, we’re likely dedicated in AWS anyway.

[01:53] Simran Kaur: Great. Elena, can you describe your “must have” on SIEM export? Like what would make you say “yes this is production-ready enough.”
[02:02] Elena Varga: Minimum is: events are complete and we don’t lose them during downtime. If Splunk is down or throttling, we need retries and then backfill.
[02:12] Elena Varga: Second: filter controls. We don’t want a firehose of everything. Mostly admin actions, auth, key/credential changes, policy changes.
[02:22] Elena Varga: Third: EU residency. We cannot have audit logs shipped to US processing, even temporarily.

[02:30] Jonas Keller: And dedup. If it’s at-least-once, okay, but then we need a stable ID. Otherwise my team will chase ghosts.

[02:37] Colin O'Donnell: Yeah, that makes sense. Our design is at-least-once, so duplicates are possible, and we include a stable event_id for dedup downstream.
[02:46] Colin O'Donnell: We also include timestamps: when the event occurred and when it was observed/ingested, so you can do lag calculations.

[02:54] Marie Dubois: I want to ask directly: do these audit events contain prompts or model outputs?
[03:00] Naomi Feldman: No prompts or outputs in the audit event schema. It’s “audit”, so metadata about actions. For example “user X created API key”, “workspace Y changed setting”, “model route updated”, things like that.
[03:12] Naomi Feldman: There are a few fields that can be sensitive like IP and user agent; those are included only where applicable and we have redaction/minimization rules.

[03:22] Marie Dubois: Okay. IP address is personal data in EU context. So we’ll need to understand if it’s always included or optional.
[03:30] Colin O'Donnell: It’s not on every event. It’s tied to certain actor types (like console login) and request context. We can also discuss whether you want to filter those out at export.
[03:42] Elena Varga: Filtering out IP might hurt incident response though. We might want to keep it for admin logins at least.

[03:50] Simran Kaur: That’s a common tradeoff. We’ll send the field list and the policy doc so you can decide.

[04:00] Simran Kaur: On destinations, Jonas you said Splunk and Datadog. Which do you want first for the POC?
[04:07] Jonas Keller: Long term Splunk. But practically, our Splunk team is slow. We could do S3 and then forward from there. We already have pipelines from S3 into Splunk.
[04:18] Tomás Ribeiro: Yeah, S3 in our AWS account, EU region, encrypted with our KMS key. That’s easiest.

[04:27] Colin O'Donnell: Great. S3 is one of our first-class destinations. We support server-side encryption, including SSE-KMS. We can do cross-account assume role too.
[04:38] Tomás Ribeiro: Cross-account assume role is fine. But it must be least privilege and EU-only endpoints.

[04:46] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. We have an allowlist on destination hosts for network egress for the HTTP-based adapters. For S3 it’s AWS APIs. We can pin to regional endpoints.
[04:57] Tomás Ribeiro: Okay.

[05:00] Simran Kaur: Let’s dig into residency. When you say EU-only, is it: data stored in EU, and processed in EU, and support access from EU only? Or what’s your policy exactly?
[05:13] Marie Dubois: For this control, the hard requirement is: the audit event data cannot leave the EU in transit or at rest. Support access is separate but we prefer it’s restricted.
[05:25] Marie Dubois: If you process events in the US even briefly, that fails.

[05:31] Naomi Feldman: Understood. For beta, our intent is: if your Redwood tenant is in an EU region, the exporter runs in-region and writes to your EU bucket or EU Splunk endpoint.
[05:44] Naomi Feldman: I do want to be careful: the control plane for configuration is global, but the actual event payloads and delivery pipeline are region-scoped.

[05:54] Elena Varga: Wait, “config is global” — does that mean the audit events could pass through global services?

[06:01] Colin O'Donnell: The config is like “where to send” and “what filters.” That metadata is small and doesn’t include the event stream.
[06:09] Colin O'Donnell: The event stream itself is produced in the region and consumed by the exporter in-region.

[06:16] Marie Dubois: We’ll need that in writing. It’s always a question from procurement.
[06:20] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can provide a short architecture statement and we can point to where the exporter is deployed.

[06:28] Jonas Keller: Also, we will ask for evidence. Like SOC2 report won’t answer this level.
[06:33] Simran Kaur: Makes sense.

[06:35] Simran Kaur: On delivery semantics: Colin, can you explain how “not losing events” works? But in plain English.
[06:42] Colin O'Donnell: Sure. The exporter reads from our audit event stream and writes in batches to the destination. We checkpoint progress per tenant and destination. If a batch fails—like 403, 429, timeouts—we retry with backoff.
[06:58] Colin O'Donnell: If it keeps failing beyond thresholds, we can dead-letter the batch and surface an error. You can replay from DLQ with an operator tool.
[07:09] Jonas Keller: So it’s not exactly-once.
[07:12] Colin O'Donnell: Correct. It’s at-least-once. So you might get duplicates. That’s why event_id exists.
[07:18] Jonas Keller: No ordering guarantees I assume.
[07:21] Colin O'Donnell: Ordering is best-effort, but you should rely on timestamps and event_id, not strict order.

[07:28] Elena Varga: What’s the event_id format? Is it stable across replays?
[07:33] Colin O'Donnell: Yes. It’s generated at emission time and it’s stable. So if we replay, you get the same ID.

[07:40] Tomás Ribeiro: For S3, what is the file layout? Like one object per event or batched?
[07:47] Colin O'Donnell: Batched. We write newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON). The path is partitioned by tenant/workspace and time. Something like: s3://bucket/redwood_audit/tenant=<id>/dt=2025-04-02/hour=14/part-0001.ndjson.
[08:06] Tomás Ribeiro: That’s good.

[08:08] Marie Dubois: Does the NDJSON include any payload that could contain user content? Like prompt strings accidentally?
[08:15] Naomi Feldman: Not by design, and we have a policy that prohibits putting prompts/outputs in audit logs. There’s also a review checklist for any new event type.
[08:26] Elena Varga: Okay, but we need to trust that. We’ll want to inspect sample events.
[08:30] Simran Kaur: Totally. We can send example payloads and in the POC you’ll validate live.

[08:37] Jonas Keller: Categories—do you have a taxonomy? Like auth, admin, data access, etc.
[08:43] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Categories like authentication, authorization, workspace_admin, api_key, billing, model_management, deployment, things along those lines. We can share the list.
[08:56] Elena Varga: Filtering: can we do allowlist by category and then maybe actions?
[09:02] Colin O'Donnell: That’s exactly how it works. You can allowlist categories, and optionally specify actions. There’s also denylist if you want default-include then exclude. But most security teams start with allowlist.
[09:15] Tomás Ribeiro: Where is filtering evaluated? In the exporter or earlier?
[09:20] Colin O'Donnell: In beta it’s evaluated in the exporter, using the config synced from the control plane.
[09:28] Tomás Ribeiro: Okay. Performance impact?
[09:31] Colin O'Donnell: Minimal. It’s basically JSON predicate checks.

[09:38] Simran Kaur: Let’s talk about “what success looks like.” Jonas, Elena—if we did a 2-week POC, what are the explicit checks you’d run?
[09:48] Jonas Keller: For me: I want to see events arrive in our S3 within, say, five minutes of occurrence. And if we block S3 permissions or throttle, I want to see it recover and backfill.
[10:02] Jonas Keller: Also want a dashboard or at least an endpoint that shows lag and last error.

[10:08] Elena Varga: I want to see RBAC. Like only security admins can set up export destinations. Developers shouldn’t be able to add a random HTTP endpoint and exfiltrate.
[10:18] Elena Varga: Also credential handling. Where are secrets stored.

[10:23] Marie Dubois: For me it’s the data mapping: which fields are personal, whether IP is present, and retention. How long you keep audit events on your side and how long export can backfill.

[10:35] Naomi Feldman: On retention: we retain audit logs in Redwood for a set period depending on plan; export is not a replacement for retention, it’s delivery. For beta, backfill window is limited—currently we’re targeting up to 7 days.
[10:51] Naomi Feldman: We should align on that so there’s no surprises.

[10:55] Jonas Keller: 7 days is okay for POC. For prod we’d want longer, but we can ingest continuously.

[11:02] Simran Kaur: On visibility: in the Console there’s an “Audit Export” settings page with status. Also we have metrics like export lag, retries, error rate.
[11:12] Jonas Keller: Can we access that via API too?
[11:15] Colin O'Donnell: There is a status endpoint the Console uses. We can expose it to your admins.

[11:22] Elena Varga: RBAC names? Like do you have a role “audit export admin”?
[11:26] Naomi Feldman: We have permissions specifically for managing audit exports and viewing delivery status. Not everyone gets it by default.
[11:34] Elena Varga: Okay.

[11:36] Tomás Ribeiro: If we do S3 cross-account assume role, do you support external ID? We require it.
[11:42] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, we support external ID in the assume-role flow.
[11:47] Tomás Ribeiro: And policy should limit to a prefix.
[11:50] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, we recommend restricting to a path prefix and specific bucket.

[11:57] Marie Dubois: Where are the destination credentials stored? If it’s an IAM role it’s not a secret, but for Splunk tokens it is.
[12:05] Colin O'Donnell: For S3, it’s role-based. For Splunk/Datadog keys, we store secrets encrypted at rest and we redact them from logs. The config references a secret ID, not the plaintext.
[12:18] Elena Varga: Good.

[12:20] Simran Kaur: Can you confirm which Redwood deployment you’re evaluating? Hosted API or dedicated?
[12:26] Tomás Ribeiro: Dedicated. We want dedicated GPUs and tenant isolation anyway. Region would be Frankfurt, probably.
[12:33] Simran Kaur: That aligns. Beta covers dedicated.

[12:37] Naomi Feldman: Small note: private deployments not in beta. But dedicated in EU region is fine.
[12:43] Tomás Ribeiro: Understood.

[12:45] Simran Kaur: Let’s also cover volume. Jonas, roughly how many audit events do you expect? Like number of Redwood users, number of admin actions.
[12:55] Jonas Keller: Hard to say. Admin actions are low. But API usage could be high; do you emit audit events for every inference request?

[13:04] Naomi Feldman: For audit logs, we do not log every inference token request as an audit event. It’s more control-plane and security relevant actions.
[13:12] Naomi Feldman: There may be some “API key used” style events depending on configuration, but we’re careful to avoid high-cardinality firehose.

[13:22] Elena Varga: That’s good. We don’t want 10 million events per day.

[13:26] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly. For SIEM use, it’s mostly “who did what” for admin/security changes.

[13:33] Marie Dubois: Can we get a list of event types you currently emit?
[13:38] Simran Kaur: We can share the taxonomy plus a set of sample events.

[13:43] Tomás Ribeiro: On the EU-only requirement: if your control plane is global, what about the UI calls? Like when we view status, does it pull event data?
[13:52] Colin O'Donnell: Status is aggregate metrics and last error text, not the raw event stream.
[13:58] Tomás Ribeiro: Okay.

[14:00] Elena Varga: What about support access to troubleshoot? Would your SREs in the US see the audit payload?
[14:06] Simran Kaur: Typically SREs see metrics and logs about the exporter health, not the raw event payloads. We can also discuss support access controls. But for beta we can commit to limiting what’s logged.
[14:18] Naomi Feldman: And our audit event policy is to minimize sensitive payload fields. We can walk through it.

[14:26] Jonas Keller: Does the exporter have a DLQ we can see? Like if things fail for hours.
[14:31] Colin O'Donnell: We have internal DLQ and a replay tool. For customers, we surface the error state and can coordinate a replay. In beta, we might keep replay as a Redwood-operated action.
[14:44] Jonas Keller: That’s fine for beta.

[14:47] Simran Kaur: Okay. Let me propose a POC checklist based on what you said, and you tell me if it matches.
[14:54] Simran Kaur: One: configure S3 destination in eu-central-1, cross-account role with external ID, SSE-KMS with your CMK.
[15:03] Simran Kaur: Two: configure filters allowlisting security/admin categories, exclude anything you deem too noisy.
[15:10] Simran Kaur: Three: validate delivery: events show up within target lag under normal operation.
[15:15] Simran Kaur: Four: failure test: we intentionally break the role policy for 15 minutes, confirm exporter retries, then restore and confirm it backfills without manual work.
[15:26] Simran Kaur: Five: dedup test: we trigger a replay scenario and confirm event_id is stable in your pipeline.
[15:33] Simran Kaur: Six: documentation/evidence: provide you an architecture statement about EU processing, plus the schema and PII policy.

[15:43] Elena Varga: That covers it.
[15:45] Jonas Keller: Add one more: we need an operational view. Even if it’s just the status endpoint and what metrics exist.
[15:52] Colin O'Donnell: Yep, we can include that.

[15:55] Marie Dubois: And I need a clear answer on IP and user agent: are they collected, and can we disable them?
[16:02] Naomi Feldman: We can’t promise “disable collection” for all events in beta, but we can filter them out at export for certain categories if that satisfies your policy. We should check what fields are emitted per event type.
[16:16] Marie Dubois: Filtering out might be sufficient, as long as you don’t ship them out of the region.

[16:22] Tomás Ribeiro: S3 path prefix, can we choose it?
[16:25] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, you can set a prefix. We recommend something like /redwood/audit/.

[16:31] Elena Varga: Another question: can developers create their own export destination?
[16:36] Naomi Feldman: No, it’s permission-gated. It’s a privileged admin action. We can review your desired role mapping.

[16:44] Jonas Keller: What about multiple destinations? Like S3 and Splunk at same time.
[16:48] Colin O'Donnell: Supported. Each destination has its own checkpoint and health.

[16:54] Tomás Ribeiro: Any limits on number of destinations?
[16:57] Naomi Feldman: In beta we might cap it to keep operations sane—like a small number per tenant. But S3 plus one other is fine.

[17:06] Simran Kaur: Quick timeline: when do you need this by?
[17:10] Elena Varga: We have an internal gate in late April. If we can show a working POC by then, we can proceed with the platform rollout.

[17:19] Naomi Feldman: That’s tight but possible. Our beta is already running internally. For external customers, we’re onboarding through April.

[17:27] Simran Kaur: Great.

[17:28] (crosstalk)
[17:29] Jonas Keller: Sorry—what’s the current state, like is it stable?
[17:32] Colin O'Donnell: It’s beta. It’s stable enough for controlled use, but we’ve seen typical downstream throttling issues. That’s why we have backoff and a max lag safety that can pause exports.
[17:46] Jonas Keller: Pause exports meaning it stops sending?
[17:49] Colin O'Donnell: Yes, if lag exceeds a threshold it can auto-pause to avoid runaway retries. We surface that state.
[17:58] Elena Varga: Pausing is okay as long as we can resume and backfill.
[18:02] Colin O'Donnell: Exactly.

[18:05] Tomás Ribeiro: If it pauses, do you drop events?
[18:08] Colin O'Donnell: No, events remain in the source stream and we resume from checkpoint.

[18:14] Marie Dubois: Deletion semantics: if we delete a user, does their name stay in audit logs?
[18:20] Naomi Feldman: Audit logs are typically immutable for compliance. We don’t rewrite historical audit. But we minimize PII. We can discuss what fields represent the actor—usually an internal ID plus display name.
[18:34] Marie Dubois: Okay, we’ll need to document that.

[18:38] Simran Kaur: I think we have enough to proceed. Next, Colin can set up a 30-minute technical session focused on the S3 IAM/KMS config.
[18:47] Colin O'Donnell: Yep. Tomás, I’ll send a minimal IAM policy template. We’ll need: assume role trust with external ID, permissions for PutObject to a prefix, and KMS encrypt permissions for that key.
[19:02] Tomás Ribeiro: Good. We’ll use a dedicated role.

[19:06] Elena Varga: And you’ll send sample events so we can pre-review categories.
[19:10] Simran Kaur: Yes.

[19:12] Naomi Feldman: Also, to be clear: beta backfill is limited. If you don’t have export running for months, we can’t reconstruct everything. But within the backfill window, you can replay.
[19:25] Jonas Keller: Understood.

[19:28] Simran Kaur: I’m going to skip ahead a bit—anything else blocking that we didn’t cover?
[19:34] Elena Varga: One concern: can you guarantee you won’t send to a non-EU bucket by misconfiguration? Like guardrails.
[19:41] Colin O'Donnell: For S3, we validate bucket region. For HTTP endpoints (Splunk/Datadog), we validate hostname against allowlist patterns. For residency, we can also add checks to prevent non-EU destinations if your tenant is EU-only. I need to confirm what’s available in beta.
[20:00] Naomi Feldman: We do have destination validation hooks. We can treat EU residency as a policy requirement in your config—at least by process, and potentially by validation.

[20:12] Tomás Ribeiro: Okay, we want that. “Process” is less good than “technical control,” but for beta it might be acceptable.
[20:20] Simran Kaur: We’ll document what’s enforced and what’s contractual/process.

[20:25] (brief pause)

[20:27] Jonas Keller: Sorry, one more—how do we dedup in S3? Like do you guarantee no duplicates within a file?
[20:34] Colin O'Donnell: Duplicates could appear across files, and in rare cases within a retry scenario you might see overlap. The recommended dedup key is event_id. When you ingest into Splunk, set that as the unique key.
[20:48] Jonas Keller: Okay.

[20:50] Simran Kaur: Great. Since we have time, Naomi can you quickly outline what fields are in the audit schema, just high level?
[20:58] Naomi Feldman: Sure. It’s: event_id, event_time, observed_time, tenant/workspace identifiers, actor (user/service), action, resource, and then context like source_ip and user_agent when applicable.
[21:14] Naomi Feldman: We also include a category field for filters and for SIEM mapping.

[21:20] Elena Varga: Actor includes email?
[21:22] Naomi Feldman: Usually we store an internal user_id and display name. Email is generally avoided in audit payloads; we can confirm on the exact fields for the events you care about.

[21:33] Marie Dubois: Please confirm. Email in logs is always a sensitive topic.
[21:37] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[21:40] Tomás Ribeiro: On encryption: S3 SSE-KMS, fine. In transit: TLS.
[21:45] Colin O'Donnell: Correct.

[21:47] Simran Kaur: Let’s do a quick recap and assign next steps.

[21:52] Simran Kaur: Redwood: we’ll send you (1) security FAQ and retention/export responsibilities language, (2) schema v2 examples and category list, (3) S3 IAM/KMS templates, and (4) a short statement on EU-region processing for audit export.
[22:10] Simran Kaur: Quantiva: you’ll confirm the target EU region for the bucket and whether you need eu-west-1 vs eu-central-1, and you’ll estimate expected audit volume and key event categories.
[22:22] Simran Kaur: Then we schedule the technical validation session early next week.

[22:28] Elena Varga: Works.
[22:29] Tomás Ribeiro: Yep.
[22:30] Marie Dubois: Fine.
[22:31] Jonas Keller: Yep.

[22:34] Simran Kaur: Anything else before we drop?
[22:37] Jonas Keller: No, thanks.

[22:40] Colin O'Donnell: Thanks everyone.

[22:42] Naomi Feldman: Thank you.

[22:44] Simran Kaur: Alright, we’ll follow up by Friday. Bye.

(Transcript ends)

Note: Fireflies transcript may omit some mid-call discussion due to cross-talk and audio drops; key decisions and next steps captured above.
